extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, in-house counsel, judges and practitioners handling civil patent disputes in the Republic of Korea
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for conducting civil patent/utility model litigation in Korea, covering technical assistance, evidence handling, ADR, and remedies (injunctions, damages, employee invention compensation). Intended to guide practitioners and courts on procedural and substantive criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of judicial technical examiners
rubrics_metrics.description: Each patent case of the Patent Court has a judicial technical examiner having expertise in the field assigned to the case, and the judicial panel holds a technical explanatory session before the trial, during which the judicial technical examiner helps the judges to understand the technical issues of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial technical examiners may participate in preparatory hearings and trials, ask questions to parties with the presiding judge's permission, and explain relevant technologies using demonstrative materials. They are full-time court employees distinct from case-by-case external advisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment and function of technical advisors
rubrics_metrics.description: The court may appoint a technical advisor from a pool of registered experts in a wide variety of technical fields to provide expert opinion on particular issues of a case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical advisors can submit written opinions or attend trial to provide explanations or opinions and, with permission, ask questions to parties or witnesses. They are bound by confidentiality obligations and are deemed government employees for bribery provisions. They differ from judicial technical examiners by being outside professionals appointed on a case-by-case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-trial internal technical explanatory session
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial panels of the Patent Court hold technical explanatory sessions in preparation of trials concerning patents or utility models to better understand the relevant technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At these sessions, technical experts (e.g., judicial technical examiners) explain technologies in the context of the party’s argument using drawings, products, miniatures, computer graphics and video equipment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology review session on the date of trial (materials and submission)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the trial date, in cases involving complex technical issues, technology review sessions are often held in which each party or its counsel prepares presentation materials and explains the relevant technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties are advised to submit materials for technology review prior to the trial date; materials (PDF, slideshow, video files, photographs, drawings) often become part of the court record once filed. Electronic submission is customary; trials may be conducted in a foreign language with parties' consent and court approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited access to trade secrets in court records
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon a party’s request, the court can order that only the parties to the lawsuit may access or copy the portions containing trade secrets in the court record or request delivery of authentic/certified copies or abstracts of those portions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction applies to access/copying of court records but cannot by itself prevent a party from divulging trade secrets learned in litigation; other measures (e.g., confidentiality protective orders) may be needed for broader protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality protective order (trade secret protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Article 14-4 of the Unfair Competition Prevention and Trade Secret Protection Act, a party may petition the court to issue a confidentiality protective order to prevent unauthorized disclosure of trade secrets disclosed in litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'trade secret' is information of technical or business nature that is generally unknown, has independent economic value, and whose secrecy is maintained through substantial efforts. The petition must establish that submitted or to-be-submitted materials contain trade secrets and that disclosure would likely impede the party's business; specify persons to be bound; and identify the trade secrets. Orders can prohibit use or disclosure outside the litigation (including cross-use in other lawsuits). Violation may lead to criminal punishment (imprisonment up to five years or fine up to KRW 50,000,000) but only after complaint by the order-requesting party.

rubrics_metrics.name: In camera review and protective measures for submitted documents
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party refuses to produce a document on the grounds it contains confidential information, the court may order the party to present the document for in camera review so it remains sealed from the other party or third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the court orders submission to decide on production obligations, it must take measures to protect the document from disclosure; neither parties nor their counsel can participate in in camera review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial scheduling and evidence exchange practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A civil patent lawsuit typically involves a series of trial dates for oral arguments three to five weeks apart; the first trial date identifies disputed issues and holds a technology review; subsequent dates address remaining issues, evidence examination or witness examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the end of each date the court schedules the next date and notifies what issues should be addressed; parties should submit briefs and evidence in advance for the court’s review. The court renders its decision in three to four weeks after the trial is closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and classification of ADR (settlement, mediation, arbitration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative dispute resolution (ADR) refers to legal means of resolving disputes without litigation and trial, classified into judicial, administrative and private ADR, and method-wise into settlement, mediation and arbitration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features differ from litigation regarding participation (voluntary v. involuntary), effect of adjudication (agreement v. judgment), disclosure (nondisclosure for ADR), formality and scope (national v. international). The page compares features in a table to guide choice of ADR method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement in litigation (form and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'settlement in litigation' is an agreement reached before the judge during a pending lawsuit and may be reached at any time while the lawsuit is pending (including appellate or Supreme Court stages prior to final confirmation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In principle, a settlement in litigation must be reached by the parties' verbal statement in court to have the same effect as a final and conclusive judgment; a notarized brief expressing intent to settle may also constitute a settlement if the other party appears in court and accepts it on the hearing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of settlement in litigation (res judicata and executory force)
rubrics_metrics.description: When stated in the court record for trial, a settlement in litigation has the same effect as a final and conclusive judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a settlement closes the lawsuit and its record serves as the source of executory force for compulsory execution. The settlement has res judicata effect and neither party may assert its nullity between themselves except by quasi-retrial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court recommendation of settlement and its effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A court, commissioned judge or entrusted judge may render ex officio a ruling of settlement recommendation to fairly settle the case by taking account of parties’ interests and all circumstances within the gist of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A ruling of settlement recommendation has the same effect as a judicial settlement when neither party raises an objection within two weeks of receiving the ruling (or the objection is withdrawn/waived). Courts may render such recommendations even after closing of argument but before pronouncing judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediation institutions and proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediation is a dispute resolution method where a neutral third party helps parties settle the dispute; mediation may be conducted by mediation judges, standing commissioners, mediation councils, the court handling the lawsuit, or external institutions entrusted by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mediation may be initiated by a party's request or court referral; proceedings usually take place in mediation chambers but may be elsewhere; proceedings may be sealed; mediation reached is put into record and has same effect as judicial settlement. A 'ruling in lieu of mediation' (mandatory mediation ruling) can have settlement effect if not objected to within two weeks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Court mediation council composition and management
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Court operates a mediation council consisting of legal professionals and technical experts and has a mediation judge system to manage mediation cases systematically and facilitate early mediation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Patent Court may also entrust external institutions (e.g., Korean Commercial Arbitration Board) to handle mediation through memorandums of understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitration agreement formation and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: An arbitration agreement takes effect when parties agree in writing to settle by arbitration all or part of a dispute; its effectiveness is determined by overall consideration of Arbitration Act meaning, nature and form of the agreement, clause content and background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optional arbitration clauses take effect when a party opts for arbitration and the other participates without objection. If a defendant raises the existence of a valid arbitration agreement, the court should dismiss a filed action unless the agreement is null, inoperative, or incapable of being performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of civil remedies for patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A right holder is mainly entitled to two forms of relief from patent infringement – injunction and damages – which may be sought together or separately; other remedies include measures necessary to reinstate goodwill or reputation and compensation for employee inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff should choose and plead remedies appropriately; for recovery of goodwill, specifics of remedies (e.g., contents, size, font of advertisements) must be specified in the complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee invention compensation rights and overview
rubrics_metrics.description: An employee invention is an invention made by an employee in connection with their duties falling within scope of the employer’s business; an employer is automatically entitled to a free nonexclusive license, and where the employer succeeds rights or gets an exclusive license, the employee is entitled to fair compensation under the Invention Promotion Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensation provisions intersect civil law, labor law and patent law and are compulsory provisions to protect employees. Defenses to compensation claims include statute of limitations (10 years) and prior amounts paid that should be deducted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements plaintiff must prove for employee invention compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff must contend and prove (i) that they invented the employee invention; (ii) that the defendant employer succeeded to the patent/utility model/design right (or rights to acquire them); (iii) that the employer earned sole and exclusive profits generated by the employee invention; and (iv) the scope of compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove inventorship: establish employee status, that the invention falls within the employer's business and present/past duties, and that the plaintiff contributed to completion (e.g., suggesting/contributing concrete ideas, embodying ideas through experiments, providing specific means/methods, or providing detailed advice/guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors and formula for calculating compensation for employee inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Invention Promotion Act sets forth factors for calculation: A. profits the employer anticipates obtaining; B. employee's ratio of contribution with respect to employer; C. if joint invention, employee's ratio among co-inventors; D. if invention is component of multicomponent product, contribution to final product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculation formula: A × B × C × D (amount of employer’s profits × ratio of employee’s contribution vs employer × ratio among co-inventors × ratio to final product). A is calculated by product sales revenue × hypothetical royalty rate × contribution ratio of exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements required for a permanent injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: There are five elements to a permanent injunction: (1) the person seeking an injunction must be the patentee (registered when argument at fact-finding trial is closed); (2) the party subject to the order (the infringer); (3) the infringing act must be practicing the patented invention for business purposes; (4) the plaintiff must specify the infringing act and the defendant’s duty to disclose the specific act; (5) infringement or likelihood of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonexclusive licensees lack standing to seek injunctions. If defendant disputes specified acts, burden of proof rests on plaintiff; the Patent Act requires defendant to disclose actual conduct and court may deem plaintiff's specification true if defendant fails to present conduct without justifiable reason. Practicing for business includes nonprofit operations; personal/household use does not constitute infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limitations of permanent injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Scope involves (a) claim for an injunction (court often issues default injunction to prohibit infringing practices), (b) claim for disposal of infringing products (must accompany injunction and be clearly specified), and (c) other measures necessary to prevent infringement (must be balanced to avoid excessive burden).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If patented invention is part/component of defendant’s product, issues arise whether injunction covers whole product and whether destruction of whole product can be claimed. Courts may issue injunctions only against infringing parts and order destruction of manufacturing equipment. Example injunction language is provided for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory basis and elements for damages claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 128(1) allows a patentee or exclusive licensee to claim compensation for damages caused by a person who has willfully or negligently infringed the patent or exclusive license; damages claims generally follow tort principles, requiring proof of (i) plaintiff is patentee; (ii) infringer willfully or negligently infringed; (iii) infringement unlawful; (iv) infringer capable of liability; (v) patentee suffered damages; (vi) proximate causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent infringement is presumed negligent under the Patent Act. The 2019 amendment allows courts to enhance damages up to three times actual damages if infringement is willful. Claimant must identify alleged infringer; actions based on unjust enrichment have a 10-year limitation; general damages actions must be filed within 3 years from awareness or within 10 years from date of infringement, whichever earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who can be a defendant and joint liability for damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant is usually the direct infringer; indirect infringers under Article 127 and persons who aided or abetted infringement may also be liable; where infringement is divided among multiple parties, joint tort principles may apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial views differ whether objective joint tort (only acts jointly occurred) suffices or subjective joint tort (knowledge/conspiracy to act jointly) is required. Courts may apportion damages proportionally among co-right-holders for jointly owned patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds and methods for calculating damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act recognizes four grounds in assessing damages: (i) loss suffered by the patentee (lost profits); (ii) profits earned by the infringer (presumed to equal damages); (iii) reasonable royalty (at minimum); (iv) damages determined at court’s discretion based on overall examination of evidence (discretionary damages where actual damages are hard to prove).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lost profits: for units within patentee’s production capacity, calculate number of units times profit per unit. The amended Act (Dec 10, 2020) permits recovery of reasonable royalty for units transferred by infringer that exceed patentee's production capacity (royalty pursuant to Article 128(5)). Discretionary damages may be awarded where evidentiary proof of actual damages is difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits and recovery for units exceeding patentee's production capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: For units within the patentee’s production capacity, lost profits may be awarded for units the patentee would have sold but for the infringement; units outside production capacity are excluded from lost profits calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The amended Patent Act allows recovery of reasonable royalty for infringer-transferred units that exceed the patentee’s production capacity or could not be sold due to reasons other than infringement. The royalty amount is equivalent to that prescribed in Article 128(5).
